title: How They Cure Ne'erdoweels
text: THE story of Jerry Guttridge, which was presented a few weeks ago in the Journal, furnished on the whole not a bad plan for "pulling up" that numerous class of beings usually known among us under the names of ne'erdoweels," " victims," and "downdraughts." I do not certainly recommend whipping as a means for curing either habitual drunkenness or idleness, for, independently of the cruelty of such a mode of punishment, it has generally the effect of hardening instead of mollifying the evil dispositions of offenders. Ne'erdoweels must be treated very much like persons who labour under mental alienation. Their faculties and tastes are diseased. They are, in some respects, not accountable for their behaviour any more than an idiot or lunatic. As things go with us, ne'erdoweels are subject to no species of judicial control. Their friends and relatives have no power whatever to place them legally in confinement. An honest and worthy man may be worried to death with a drunken wife or a vicious good-for-nothing son, but the law offers no means of relief. We hear daily of of the most distressing cases of wives and families being in a state of destitution, in consequence of husbands and fathers spending their earnings in reckless intemperance, but neither magistrates nor correctional police have any thing to say in the matter. A man may allow his family to become a burden on society, but society can only complain of the injustice. With the greatest respect for civil liberty, we cannot help thinking that there is something wrong here; and it becomes a very grave question, whether, in maintaining the principle of personal freedom, we do not, in this instance at least, go a little too far, and incur evils on the other side.

In Holland, and some of the German states (perhaps in all), it is competent for the public authorities to deprive any man of his liberty, and send him to the house of correction, on a due representation of his being guilty of habitual idleness, drunkenness, or general bad behaviour. Cases of ne'erdoweelisın and victimisation are consequently rare in Holland, and assuredly are not observable on the common thoroughfares, as we see them in this country. In Prussia, when a man addicts himself to habits of intemperance, and regularly misspends the earnings which should go to the maintenance of his family, the public authorities take cognisance of his conduct. He is pulled up. On being brought before a magistrate, we may suppose him to be addressed in the following terms:-"You are here, sir, on the very serious charge of being an habitual drunkard. The wages which you earn, when it pleases your fancy you regularly spend upon liquor your wife and are at the point of starvation; they have neither fuel, and their clothing is insufficient for their This conduct is infamous, for you are a good and could earn six thalers per week, on which and family might live in great comfort and I say your behaviour is intolerable; you are a sance, for your example inay seduce others to the same career of wickedness; and in the you are leaving your family to be a burthen on and industrious men. But this shall continue no I consign you to the house of correction, where be removed from all temptations to vice, and opportunity of working for your family, and of resolutions to amend your life for the future." Thus tured on his delinquency, the ne'erdoweel is handed prison. He is then set to work, as far as it can be in the kind of employment he has been accustomed and a certain portion of his weekly earnings is to his family. What may be the length of his ment, I am not aware; most likely it varies the circumstances of the case, and the appearance amendment. The object being to reclaim, not to no undue harshness is employed.

During my stay in Holland, I heard of the practice incarcerating and reclaiming ne'erdoweels. At dam there are several apartinents within the of the Dol Huis, or lunatic asylum, which are for this purpose. On the representation of guardians, or other relatives or friends, or by for the public interest, all dissolute and abandoned racters, confirmed drunkards, whether male or are consigned for correction to the Dol Huis, where houseless vagrants, youths who haunt the public roughfares, and can show no honest means of ence, and others in a deserted miserable condition taken hold of by the police, and sent off to one or of the great industrial penitentiaries, called "home nies," in a distant part of the country. In Amsterdam there is a similar asylum or prison. (Maison de for the incarceration of ne'erdoweels of both sexes which is also useful as a house of refuge, or place which work and subsistence may be had for a short riod by persons in destitute circumstances.
These continental practices might not be suitable in this country, but they afford a hint for thing of the kind; and the subject is of such importance as to be well worthy of consideration.
